summary: A survey of the state of graphics on the ARPANET for newcomers. It reviews past work, notes how little had been written on the subject, and adds the author's own thoughts about using the network's many computers for graphics.

plainLanguage.summary: An overview of how people were using the network for pictures so far, and where they might go next.

questions: what is network graphics on the arpanet
what is attention handling in graphics
subtitle: A newcomer's survey of ARPANET graphics proposals, plus a simple model of how a graphics system could fit together.

tldr.problem: Little had been written about graphics on the ARPANET, and earlier proposals dealt with details without a general model of the whole system.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys the earlier work and then proposes a model with a PROCESS, input and output routines, input and output display drivers, a DISPLAY, and two graphic data bases, linked by a network standard graphics protocol.
tldr.outcome: It prioritizes the widest mix of configurations over minimum response time. The RFC lists its status as Unknown.

today: The RFC's status is listed as Unknown, and it neither updates nor is updated by another RFC according to the metadata. It is a December 1971 discussion paper and its model is a proposal rather than a specified protocol.

sections.title: Why a Survey
sections.content:
The NIC collection held some 8000 entries, of which only about 20 were on graphics. The author compares this to a point made by L. G. Roberts, that the net had not been up long enough for people to know what was feasible. The paper is aimed at newcomers: an overview, a short account of past work, then the author's own thoughts.

Because the net offers many computers, a more powerful machine may act as the display processor than the one running the main job. The processor that builds a display list for one specific terminal translates a general language for that terminal only.
sections.plainLanguage: Hardly anyone had written about network pictures yet, so this paper collects what exists and adds a plan.

sections.title: What Earlier Proposals Said
sections.content:
Early Network Standard Graphics proposals began with a small interpretable language: erase, display text, move, draw, run a subroutine and redefine one. Critics said a standard had to use all present and foreseeable graphics hardware, so it grew into a general high-level language. Its basic list includes points, lines, vectors, character strings, viewport and window, transformations of instances, hardware-dependent byte streams and attention commands.

Other work covered a Graphics Loader for the LDS-1 processor at M.I.T., tablet input data in four types (single-shot, raw asynchronous, raw synchronous and preprocessed), and NETCRT, a protocol for a character display that is slaved to a central processor. Attention handling means reporting the user's actions at the display back to the program.
sections.plainLanguage: First people wanted a few easy drawing commands, but then they wanted to use every kind of screen, so the plan grew bigger.

sections.title: The Proposed Model
sections.content:
The model has a PROCESS, the graphics application program, with INPUT and OUTPUT routines. At the other end are INPUT and OUTPUT drivers for the DISPLAY. Drawing information flows from the PROCESS to the DISPLAY, and attention information flows back. Each side has its own Graphic Data Base, so the OUTPUT driver can handle attentions without the main PROCESS.

Two modes follow. In PROGRAM graphics the main PROCESS builds the picture and the display's data base is updated afterwards. In LOCAL graphics the user draws with function buttons and the display data base updates at once, with the PROCESS notified.

Graphics messages should carry a distinguishing header, then a byte giving the type of information, a count of the bytes in the body, and the body itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The program and the screen each keep their own copy of the picture and send short messages to keep the copies matching.

sections.title: Goals and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The author says the design aims at the greatest generality of configurations rather than minimum response time. The hardware and usage cannot be known in advance, so intelligent drivers should split the processing between themselves and the main PROCESS according to the kind of display, rather than build in a fixed breakpoint.

The model can be used with minimal overhead for non-interactive graphics by skipping the attention processing. The author notes that opportunities exist to use software sharing and data reconfiguration services, and that much detailed work remains.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan is built to work with any screen, not to be the fastest, because nobody knows yet which screens will be used.
